q: You are about to move off from the side of the road. What should you do?
e: Use all your mirrors, look round to check your blind spot, and signal if it would help other road users.
o: Check your mirrors and blind spot, and signal if necessary
Signal, then move off as soon as the road ahead is clear
Sound your horn so other road users know you are there
Check your interior mirror, then move off without signalling

q: What is a blind spot?
e: Blind spots are areas around your vehicle that your mirrors don't show. Look round to check them before moving off or changing lanes.
o: An area your mirrors do not show
An area your headlights do not light
A part of the road hidden by a hill
A patch of road that has no markings

q: When should you use your mirrors?
e: Use the routine mirror – signal – manoeuvre. Check your mirrors before you signal, turn or change speed.
o: Before signalling or changing speed or direction
Only when you are about to stop or slow down
Only when you are about to reverse into a space
After you have started to turn or change lanes

q: What is the main purpose of the mirror – signal – manoeuvre routine?
e: Using MSM means you know what is around you before you act, and other road users know what you intend to do.
o: To change speed or direction safely
To use less fuel on every journey
To make the gear changes smoother
To keep to the speed limit more easily

q: You are driving on a long journey and start to feel tired. What should you do?
e: If you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place. Drinking two caffeinated drinks and taking a short nap of at least 15 minutes can help.
o: Stop somewhere safe and take a rest
Open a window and carry on driving
Turn the radio up and carry on
Drive faster to finish the journey sooner

q: How often should you take a break on a long journey?
e: Plan your journey so that you take a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours.
o: Only when you feel very tired

q: You are driving on a motorway and feel very tired. What should you do?
e: You must not stop on the hard shoulder to rest. Leave the motorway at the next exit or service area.
o: Leave at the next exit or services and rest
Stop on the hard shoulder and take a rest
Stop on a slip road and take a short nap
Keep going but drive in the left-hand lane

q: When may you use a hand-held mobile phone in your car?
e: It is illegal to use a hand-held phone while driving, including when you are stopped in traffic or at lights.
o: When you are queuing in traffic
When you are waiting at traffic lights
When you are driving below 20 mph

q: What is the penalty for using a hand-held mobile phone while driving?
e: Using a hand-held phone while driving can lead to 6 penalty points and a £200 fine. New drivers can lose their licence.

q: Which statement about hands-free phones is correct?
e: Hands-free phones are legal, but they can still distract you. You can be prosecuted if you are not in proper control of your vehicle.
o: They can still distract you from driving
They are illegal to use while driving
They are safe to use at any time
They can only be used on motorways

q: You are driving and your mobile phone rings. What should you do?
e: Keep your attention on the road. Find a safe place to stop before using your phone.
o: Let it ring and return the call when parked
Answer it quickly while keeping your speed low
Stop on the hard shoulder to answer it
Answer it if you are in a traffic queue

q: When should you set your sat nav?
e: Set your sat nav before you set off. Don't let it distract you while you are driving.
o: When you stop at traffic lights
While you are in a traffic queue

q: You are approaching a bend and your view ahead is blocked. What should you do?
e: Drive at a speed that will allow you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn and keep your speed
Move to the centre of the road
Speed up to get through the bend quickly

q: You are about to turn right into a side road. What should you check just before you turn?
e: Check your right mirror and blind spot. Motorcyclists or cyclists may be overtaking you.
o: Your right mirror and blind spot
Your left mirror and blind spot

q: What should you do before you reverse?
e: Check all around before and while reversing. Small children may be hidden from view.
o: Look all around, including behind you
Sound your horn and then reverse
Switch on your hazard warning lights

q: You are reversing. Who should you be most aware of?
e: Small children are hard to see from the driving seat. If you can't see properly, get someone to guide you.
o: Small children who may be hidden from view
Cyclists on the other side of the road
Drivers waiting at a junction ahead
Lorries a long way behind you

q: When are you most likely to lose concentration?
e: Long journeys, such as on motorways, can make you lose concentration. Take regular breaks.
o: When driving through a busy town
Just after you have set off

q: Another driver flashes their headlights at you. What does the Highway Code say this means?
e: Only flash your headlights to let other road users know you are there. Never assume it is a signal to go.
o: They are letting you know they are there
They are giving way to you
They are telling you to go ahead
They are warning you about a police check

q: You want to emerge from a junction but your view is blocked. What should you do?
e: Edge forward slowly and carefully until you have a clear view. Don't rely on hearing traffic.
o: Creep forward slowly until you can see clearly
Sound your horn and pull out
Wait until you can't hear any traffic
Pull out quickly when there is a gap

q: What should you use your horn for?
e: Only use your horn while moving, to warn others of your presence. Never use it aggressively.
o: To warn others that you are there
To tell a slow driver to hurry

q: In a built-up area, between which times must you not use your horn unless a moving vehicle poses a danger?
e: Don't sound your horn in a built-up area between 11.30 pm and 7 am, or while stationary, unless a moving vehicle poses a danger.

q: Why should you look well ahead when you are driving?
e: Looking well ahead gives you time to plan and react to hazards.
o: To read the road signs only

q: Your vision becomes blurred during a long drive because you are tired. What should you do?
e: Tiredness affects your vision and concentration. Stop somewhere safe and rest.
o: Open a window and drive more slowly
Rub your eyes and carry on
Switch on the radio and carry on

q: You are waiting to emerge from a junction. The windscreen pillar is restricting your view. Who could be hidden?
e: Windscreen pillars can hide motorcyclists and cyclists. Move your head to check, and look carefully before pulling out.

q: A driver behind you is following much too closely. What should you do?
e: Leave more room in front so you can slow down gently if you need to. Don't brake suddenly.
o: Gradually increase the gap in front of you
Brake sharply to warn the driver
Speed up to get away from them
Wave at them to overtake you

q: In good conditions, what is the minimum time gap you should leave behind the vehicle in front?
e: Leave at least a two-second gap in good, dry conditions.

q: You are driving on a wet road. What gap should you leave behind the vehicle in front?
e: On wet roads the gap should be at least doubled, to at least four seconds.

q: You are following a slow-moving vehicle on a narrow, winding road. What should you do?
e: Be patient. Only overtake when it is safe and legal to do so.
o: Stay back until it is safe to overtake
Overtake on the next bend to save time
Sound your horn to get it to pull over
Keep close behind so you can overtake quickly

q: Another driver pulls out in front of you from a junction. What should you do?
e: Don't react aggressively. Stay calm and keep a safe distance.
o: Sound your horn and overtake them
Follow closely to show your annoyance

q: A pedestrian has stepped onto a zebra crossing ahead. What must you do?
e: You MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto a zebra crossing.

q: A pedestrian is waiting to cross at a zebra crossing. What should you do?
e: Look out for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop to let them cross.
o: Be ready to slow down and stop
Sound your horn to warn them
Speed up to pass before they step out

q: Why should you never wave pedestrians across the road?
e: Waving someone across could lead them into danger from other traffic.
o: Another vehicle may be coming that won't stop
It is an offence to signal to pedestrians
It could hold up the traffic behind you
Pedestrians may not understand the signal

q: A bus is signalling to pull away from a bus stop ahead. What should you do?
e: Give way to buses signalling to pull away from stops, if you can do so safely.
o: Give way to it if it is safe to do so
Accelerate to pass it before it moves
Sound your horn to warn the bus driver
Flash your headlights to make it wait

q: An emergency vehicle with flashing blue lights is behind you. What should you do?
e: Help it to pass safely, but don't break the law or endanger others, for example by mounting the kerb or going through a red light.
o: Pull over where it is safe and legal
Drive through a red light to let it pass
Speed up to keep ahead of it

q: Which vehicle may use flashing green beacons?
e: Doctors may use flashing green beacons when answering an emergency call.
o: A doctor's car on an emergency call

q: What do flashing amber beacons on a vehicle warn you about?
e: Flashing amber beacons warn of slow-moving or large vehicles, such as road gritters and tractors.
o: An emergency vehicle on a call
A doctor on an emergency call

q: Another driver makes a mistake. How should you react?
e: Everyone makes mistakes. Don't react aggressively.
o: Follow them closely for a while
Overtake them as soon as possible

q: You are in a slow-moving queue. A driver is waiting to come out of a side road. What should you do?
e: Be considerate. Letting others out can help traffic flow.
o: Let them out if it is safe
Move forward to close the gap
Sound your horn to warn them
Flash your headlights to make them wait

q: You are in a slow-moving queue of traffic. What should you do before changing lanes?
e: Motorcyclists may filter between lanes. Check your mirrors and blind spot before changing lanes or opening a door.
o: Check for motorcyclists filtering between lanes
Move across quickly before the traffic moves
Sound your horn to warn other drivers
Switch on your hazard warning lights

q: Which of these is most likely to make you drive too fast?
e: Don't let time pressure affect your driving. Allow plenty of time for your journey.
o: Driving in heavy fog on a busy road
Driving on an unlit road at night
Being well rested before a journey

q: A vehicle has stopped at a pedestrian crossing to let people cross. What must you not do?
e: You MUST NOT overtake the moving vehicle nearest the crossing, or a vehicle that has stopped to give way to pedestrians.

q: When may you use hazard warning lights?
e: Use hazard warning lights when your vehicle is stationary and temporarily obstructing traffic. On motorways and unrestricted dual carriageways you may also use them briefly to warn of a hazard ahead.
o: When stopped and temporarily obstructing traffic
When parked on double yellow lines
To thank another driver for letting you out
When driving in heavy rain or fog

q: A learner driver in front of you stalls at traffic lights. What should you do?
e: Learner drivers may make mistakes. Be patient and give them time.
o: Sound your horn to hurry them
Overtake them as soon as you can

q: You are following an older driver who is driving slowly. What should you do?
e: Older drivers may be slower to react. Be patient.
o: Be patient and allow them extra time
Sound your horn to warn them

q: A large vehicle is coming towards you on a narrow road. What should you do?
e: Be prepared to give way or pull into a passing place on narrow roads.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Speed up to get past it quickly
Flash your headlights at the driver
Sound your horn to warn the driver

q: What should you use a passing place on a single-track road for?
e: Pull into a passing place on your left, or wait opposite one on your right, to let oncoming traffic pass or traffic behind overtake. Don't park in them.
o: To park for a short time

q: You are in a queue of traffic. A junction is coming up on your left. What should you do?
e: Don't block junctions, even in slow traffic.
o: Move forward to block the junction
Sound your horn to warn other traffic
Wave a waiting driver out of the junction

q: You want to turn left just ahead. A cyclist is riding alongside you. What should you do?
e: Don't cut across cyclists going ahead when you turn left. Wait behind them.
o: Hold back and let them pass the junction
Overtake and turn left in front of them
Sound your horn so they move over
Turn left at the same time as them

q: What is the minimum legal tread depth for car tyres?
e: Car tyres must have a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the tread, around the entire tyre.

q: When should you check your tyre pressures?
e: Check tyre pressures when the tyres are cold, using the figures in the vehicle handbook.

q: Which TWO are likely to result from under-inflated tyres?
e: Incorrect tyre pressures affect steering and braking, and under-inflated tyres increase fuel consumption.

q: Your car pulls to one side when you brake. What is the most likely cause?
e: Have your brakes checked by a qualified mechanic as soon as possible.
o: The engine oil level is low

q: Your brake pedal feels spongy. What should you do?
e: A spongy brake pedal can mean a fault in the braking system. Get it checked straight away.
o: Have the brakes checked before driving on
Pump the pedal and carry on driving
Drive more slowly for the rest of the trip
Use only the parking brake to stop

q: A warning light comes on while you are driving. What should you do?
e: Know what your warning lights mean. Red usually means stop safely as soon as possible.
o: Check what it means in the handbook
Carry on if the car feels normal
Wait to see if it goes out by itself

q: Why should you keep your windscreen and lights clean?
e: Dirty windows and lights reduce visibility, especially at night and in bad weather.
o: So you can see and be seen
So the car will pass its MOT
So you will use less fuel

q: Before driving, which of these must you be able to see through clearly?
e: All windows must be clean and clear of ice, snow, condensation and dirt before you drive.
o: Only the windscreen and rear window

q: What should you do before driving in frosty weather?
e: You must be able to see clearly in all directions. Clear ice and snow from windows, lights, mirrors and number plates.
o: Clear all windows, lights and mirrors
Clear a small area of the windscreen
Drive off and let the heater clear it
Use the wipers to clear the ice

q: What is the main purpose of a correctly adjusted head restraint?
e: In a collision, a correctly adjusted head restraint helps reduce the risk of neck injury.
o: To reduce the risk of neck injury
To make the seat more comfortable
To help you see over the car in front
To stop you leaning back too far

q: Who is legally responsible for making sure a child under 14 wears a seat belt?
e: The driver is legally responsible for making sure passengers under 14 wear a seat belt or use a suitable child restraint.

q: A passenger aged 15 is not wearing a seat belt. Who is responsible?
e: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for wearing their own seat belt.

q: Until what age or height must children normally use a child restraint?
e: Children must use a suitable child restraint until they are 12 years old or 135 cm tall, whichever comes first.

q: Where must you never fit a rear-facing baby seat?
e: Never put a rear-facing baby seat in front of an active frontal airbag. The airbag could cause serious injury or death.
o: In front of an active frontal airbag
In the rear seats of a car
In a seat with a three-point belt

q: Which TWO will help to reduce your fuel consumption?
e: Correct tyre pressures, less weight and removing roof racks all help to reduce fuel consumption.
o: Keeping your tyres at the correct pressure
Carrying extra weight in the boot

q: How can you drive in an environmentally friendly way?
e: Smooth driving and planning ahead use less fuel and reduce emissions.
o: Keep the engine at high revs

q: You expect to be stopped in traffic for some time. What can you do to reduce pollution?
e: Don't leave your engine running unnecessarily while your vehicle is stationary.
o: Switch off the engine if it is safe
Keep the engine running on idle

q: How should you dispose of used engine oil?
e: Used oil is harmful to the environment. Take it to a local authority site or a garage.
o: Take it to a local authority site
Put it in your household bin

q: What is the purpose of a catalytic converter?
e: A catalytic converter reduces the toxic gases from the exhaust.
o: To cool the engine more quickly

q: Your car's exhaust is producing a lot of smoke. What should you do?
e: Excessive exhaust smoke can mean an engine fault. It also increases pollution.
o: Have the car checked and repaired
Drive faster to clear the exhaust
Open the windows and carry on
Add more oil to the engine

q: How should you normally hold the steering wheel?
e: Keep both hands on the wheel unless you are changing gear or using other controls.
o: With one hand at the top
With one hand at the bottom

q: Why should you not rest your foot on the clutch pedal while driving?
e: "Riding the clutch" causes wear and can reduce your control of the vehicle.
o: It can cause wear and reduce control
It can make the brakes less effective
It can make the engine overheat
It can make the steering heavier

q: What is coasting?
e: Coasting reduces your control of the vehicle, especially when going downhill or round bends.
o: Driving with the clutch down or in neutral
Driving slowly along a coastal road
Driving in the highest possible gear
Driving with the cruise control on

q: When should you check your engine oil level?
e: Check your oil, water, lights and tyres regularly and before a long journey.
o: Regularly and before a long journey
Only when the car is serviced
Only when a warning light comes on

q: What is most likely to make your car's steering heavy?
e: Low tyre pressures make the steering heavier.
o: A heavy load in the boot

q: What effect can a fault in the suspension have?
e: Worn or faulty suspension affects your control of the vehicle. Have it checked.

q: What is the safest way to carry a dog in a car?
e: Make sure animals are suitably restrained so they can't distract you or injure you or themselves if you stop quickly.
o: Suitably restrained, such as in a cage
On a passenger's lap in the front
Loose in the boot of a hatchback

q: Where should you park at night to help prevent theft?
e: Lock your vehicle, remove valuables and park in a well-lit area.

q: You are leaving your car for a moment. What should you do with the keys?
e: Always remove the keys and lock your vehicle, even if you are only away for a moment.
o: Remove them and lock the car

q: Your car has been damaged in a collision. What should you do before driving it again?
e: Damage you can't see may affect the brakes, steering or tyres. Have it checked if you are unsure.
o: Check only that the engine starts

q: Which mirror normally gives you the best view of the road behind?
e: Use the interior mirror first, then the door mirrors.

q: Why should you adjust your seat before driving?
e: Adjust your seat so you can reach all the controls comfortably and see clearly.
o: So you can reach all the controls
So the head restraint is lower
So the seat belt is looser

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 30 mph on a dry road?
e: At 30 mph, thinking distance is 9 metres and braking distance is 14 metres, making 23 metres in total.

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 20 mph on a dry road?
e: At 20 mph, thinking distance is 6 metres and braking distance is 6 metres, making 12 metres in total.

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 40 mph on a dry road?
e: At 40 mph, thinking distance is 12 metres and braking distance is 24 metres, making 36 metres in total.

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 50 mph on a dry road?
e: At 50 mph, thinking distance is 15 metres and braking distance is 38 metres, making 53 metres in total.

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 60 mph on a dry road?
e: At 60 mph, thinking distance is 18 metres and braking distance is 55 metres, making 73 metres in total.

q: What is the shortest overall stopping distance at 70 mph on a dry road?
e: At 70 mph, thinking distance is 21 metres and braking distance is 75 metres, making 96 metres in total.

q: What is the typical thinking distance at 30 mph?
e: Thinking distance at 30 mph is 9 metres. The braking distance is 14 metres.

q: What is the typical braking distance at 70 mph on a dry road?
e: Braking distance at 70 mph is 75 metres. Adding 21 metres thinking distance gives 96 metres overall.

q: Overall stopping distance is made up of which two parts?
e: Overall stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

q: How much longer are stopping distances likely to be on a wet road?
e: Stopping distances will be at least double on wet roads.

q: How much longer can braking distances be on an icy road?
e: In icy conditions, braking distances can be up to ten times greater than on a dry road.
o: Up to three times as long
Up to five times as long

q: Which TWO are likely to increase your thinking distance?
e: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions slow your reactions.

q: You are driving in heavy rain. What should you do?
e: Wet roads increase stopping distances and reduce visibility, so slow down and leave a much bigger gap.
o: Increase the gap from the vehicle in front
Drive closer to the vehicle in front
Switch on your hazard warning lights

q: You are driving in heavy rain and your steering suddenly becomes very light. What should you do?
e: The tyres may be losing contact with the road surface (aquaplaning). Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually.

q: You have to drive in snow. What should you do?
e: Use gentle controls and high gears to avoid wheelspin, and leave a much bigger gap.
o: Use the highest gear you can and brake gently
Use a low gear and keep the revs high
Brake firmly if you need to stop
Keep close to the vehicle in front

q: How should you drive on an icy road?
e: Gentle, smooth use of the controls helps to avoid skidding.
o: Slowly, with gentle steering and braking
At a normal speed in a low gear
With firm braking at each hazard
With the cruise control switched on

q: The rear of your car starts to skid to the right. What should you do?
e: If the rear of the vehicle skids to the right, steer immediately to the right to recover. Don't brake harshly.

q: What does an anti-lock braking system (ABS) allow you to do?
e: ABS stops the wheels locking, so you can keep steering. It does not always shorten stopping distances, especially on wet or loose surfaces.
o: Always stop in a shorter distance

q: Your car has anti-lock brakes. How should you drive in bad weather?
e: ABS is not a reason to drive faster or closer. You still need to slow down and leave a bigger gap in bad weather.
o: The same way as without ABS
Closer to the vehicle in front

q: When must you use headlights in the daytime?
e: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see for more than 100 metres.
o: Only when it is raining heavily
Only when driving on unlit roads

q: When should you switch off your rear fog lights?
e: Fog lights can dazzle others and hide your brake lights. Switch them off when visibility improves.

q: You have to drive through a flood. What should you do?
e: Drive slowly in first gear, keeping the engine speed high by slipping the clutch. Test your brakes afterwards.
o: Drive slowly in first gear with the engine speed high
Drive through as quickly as possible
Drive in a high gear with low engine speed
Switch off the engine and coast through

q: You have just driven through deep water. What should you do first?
e: Brakes may not work well when wet. Test them gently as soon as it is safe.

q: In strong winds, which TWO are most likely to be blown off course?
e: Cyclists, motorcyclists, high-sided vehicles and vehicles towing caravans are particularly affected by strong winds.

q: You are driving in very hot weather. What should you be aware of?
e: Hot weather can soften the road surface and affect grip. Keep your vehicle well ventilated.
o: The road surface may become soft
Your tyres will have more grip
Your stopping distance will be shorter

q: You are driving down a long, steep hill. How can you help to control your speed?
e: A lower gear uses engine braking and helps to stop your brakes overheating.

q: Why should you keep well back when following a large vehicle?
e: Keeping well back improves your view of the road ahead and helps the driver see you in their mirrors.
o: To get a better view of the road ahead
To use less fuel on the journey
To be able to overtake on the left
To keep out of the wind behind it

q: When is the best time to brake for a bend?
e: Brake before the bend, while the vehicle is travelling in a straight line.
o: In the middle of the bend

q: You are driving at night with full-beam headlights on. A vehicle is coming towards you. What should you do?
e: Dip your headlights so you don't dazzle oncoming drivers.

q: You are dazzled by oncoming headlights at night. What should you do?
e: If you are dazzled, slow down or stop until your eyes recover.

q: You are driving in fog. Why should you not follow closely behind the rear lights of another vehicle?
e: Following lights can give a false sense of security. Leave a big gap so you can stop in time.
o: You may be too close to stop in time
It is illegal to do so in fog

q: Why should you use the highest possible gear on an icy road?
e: On ice, use a high gear with gentle acceleration and braking to help prevent wheelspin.
o: To save fuel on the journey
To make the brakes work better

q: On a frosty morning, where is ice likely to stay longest?
e: Ice can remain longer in shaded areas, under trees and on bridges.

q: What is a developing hazard?
e: A developing hazard is something that may cause you to change speed or direction, such as a pedestrian about to step out.
o: Something that may make you change speed or direction
A vehicle parked safely by the roadside
A road sign that tells you about a bend
A bend on a quiet country road

q: A ball bounces into the road ahead. What should you do?
e: A child may run out after the ball. Slow down and be ready to stop.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn and carry on

q: You see an ice cream van parked ahead. What should you do?
e: Children may run out from behind the van without looking.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Speed up to pass it quickly
Sound your horn as you pass

q: You are passing a line of parked cars. Which TWO hazards should you look out for?
e: Leave room for a door opening and watch for people stepping out between parked cars.

q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop ahead. What should you watch out for?
e: People getting off a bus may cross the road in front of it.
o: Pedestrians crossing in front of the bus
The driver getting off the bus

q: You see a school warning sign and children near the road. What should you do?
e: Children can be unpredictable. Drive slowly.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn to warn them
Keep to the speed limit and drive on
Flash your headlights to warn them

q: A school crossing patrol shows a "Stop for children" sign. What must you do?
e: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a "Stop for children" sign.
o: Slow down and drive past carefully
Give way only if children are crossing

q: A car on a side road ahead is edging forward. What should you do?
e: The driver may pull out in front of you. Be prepared to stop.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Speed up to get past it
Flash your headlights to let it out
Sound your horn and keep going

q: Why can motorcyclists be difficult to see at junctions?
e: Motorcyclists are small and can be hidden by other vehicles or by the windscreen pillar. Look carefully.
o: They can be hidden by other vehicles
They always ride close to the kerb

q: You are driving through a town. How can shop window reflections help you?
e: Reflections can sometimes show you hazards round corners.
o: They can show hazards you can't see directly
They can show the speed limit ahead
They can show the traffic light colours
They can show your own position

q: A person with a white stick is waiting at a zebra crossing. What should you do?
e: A white stick means the person is blind or partially sighted. Be ready to stop.
o: Slow down and be ready to stop
Sound your horn to let them know
Drive past before they step out

q: You are approaching traffic lights that have been green for some time. What should you do?
e: Lights that have been green for some time are likely to change soon.
o: Move into the centre of the road

q: You are behind a cyclist on a narrow road. A lorry is coming the other way. What should you do?
e: Don't overtake unless you can give the cyclist enough room: at least 1.5 metres at speeds up to 30 mph.
o: Hold back until it is safe to overtake
Squeeze past the cyclist before the lorry
Sound your horn so the cyclist moves over
Overtake quickly while the lorry is far away

q: You are driving on a narrow country road. Which TWO hazards should you expect?
e: Country roads may have no pavements, so people may be walking in the road. Look out for horse riders, animals and farm vehicles.

q: A lorry is reversing ahead. Why should you slow down and take care?
e: Large vehicles have large blind spots. The driver may not see you.
o: The driver may not be able to see you
It is illegal to pass a reversing lorry
The lorry may suddenly speed up
Lorries always need the whole road

q: Which of these is most likely to affect your ability to spot hazards?
e: Tiredness slows your reactions and reduces your concentration.

q: You have been given some medicine. What should you do before driving?
e: Some medicines, including some for colds and hay fever, can make you drowsy. Check the label or ask your pharmacist or doctor.
o: Check if it could affect your driving
Drive as normal if you feel well

q: What is the legal drink-drive limit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: The limit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood (35 micrograms in 100 ml of breath).
o: 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood
50 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood
100 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood
20 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood

q: What is the legal drink-drive limit in Scotland?
e: Scotland's limit is lower: 50 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood (22 micrograms in 100 ml of breath).

e: The photocard must be renewed every 10 years.

q: What is the usual minimum age to drive a car on public roads?
e: You can apply for a provisional licence at 15 years 9 months, but you can usually only drive a car on the road from 17.

e: Don't give casualties anything to eat or drink. Keep them warm and reassure them.

q: You are driving in a one-way street. On which side may you pass other vehicles?

e: In a one-way street you may pass other traffic on either side.

q: Before driving after heavy snow, why should you clear snow from the roof of your car?

So the car uses less fuel
So the roof doesn't get damaged

q: What must you have before you can legally drive your car on the road? Select TWO answers.

q: When might you need to use arm signals?

q: What does an area of diagonal white stripes bordered by a broken white line mean?
